title: Living ashtpadi 18
hook: the bond of Guru and Sikh runs both ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, nihkaamee, and your line: serve and be filled. Did you do one unasked thing, and keep quiet about it? Today we close the eighteenth ashtpadi with a famous day in 1699. Day five hundred nine.

Anandpur, at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, 1699, as Sikh tradition tells it. A huge crowd. Guru Gobind Singh stands before them with a drawn sword and asks for a head. Silence. Then one man stands up. Then another, and another, until five have come forward. The Guru initiates them with amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, and names them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. Everyone expects that to be the climax. It isn't. What the Guru does next is the part Sikhs still sing about. Today: both ways.
screen: `VAISAKHI, 1699.` → `FIVE COME FORWARD.` → `WHAT THE GURU DOES NEXT.`

segments.voice: Having initiated the five, the Guru kneels before them and asks them to initiate him in the same way. The teacher takes amrit from his own students. A later poet, writing in the tradition of Bhai Gurdas, put it in a line Sikhs still sing: wonderful is Gobind Singh, himself the Guru and himself the disciple. Aape gur chela. That moment is the eighteenth ashtpadi, lived out. This week the ashtpadi showed us two directions. First, the Guru toward the Sikh: the True Guru cherishes, cleans, frees and holds the Sikh close, like his own life. Then the Sikh toward the Guru: living in the Guru's house, serving without wanting, making no show. Read separately, those could sound like a ladder: the Guru on top, giving; the Sikh below, serving. But at Anandpur the ladder becomes a circle. The Guru serves the Sikhs; the Sikhs become a kind of Guru; the Khalsa, the community, is later called the Guru Panth. Care goes down, service goes up, and then they trade places. That's what both ways means. It's also why Sikhs describe the relationship as a bond rather than fear. In that telling, a Sikh keeps the daily banis, the five articles of faith, the honest work, not as payment to a distant master but as one half of a bond in which the other half is already given. The Guru keeps faith with the Sikh. The Sikh keeps faith with the Guru. Neither half works alone. And on an ordinary day, that bond lives in very small things: one hymn read, one practice kept, one promise to the Guru not quietly dropped.
screen: `THE GURU KNEELS TO THE FIVE.` · `AAPE GUR CHELA.` · `A LADDER BECOMES A CIRCLE.` · `TWO HALVES OF ONE BOND.` · then, large: `BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one practice to keep for the Guru, or for whatever teacher or path you're walking. It can be very small: these few minutes every day; one line of a hymn each morning; a single act of honest work done carefully. Sit and decide on it. Then rest in the other half of the bond: the care others have already given you, noticed or not. Hold both halves together. The bell holds the time.
Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones Guru Gobind Singh initiated at Anandpur, who then initiated him in turn: Aape gur chela, himself Guru and disciple, care and service running both ways.
Your line: both ways. Today, keep the one practice you chose, and remember it's your half of a bond, not a payment. Day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Vaisakhi 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh initiated the Panj Pyare and then received amrit from them, and sing the line aape gur chela; the eighteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani describes the Guru's care and the Sikh's service.

tradition says he knelt and received amrit from them.

care goes one way, service the other: a bond that runs both ways.

fork.setup: you're Guru Gobind Singh. you've just initiated the first five Khalsa. what do you do next?
options: accept their bows and close the ceremony.
kneel and ask them to initiate you.
fork.reveal: tradition says he took amrit from them: aape gur chela, himself the Guru and himself the disciple.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chela, disciple, as in aape gur chela, himself Guru and disciple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru leads and the Sikh follows. end of story.
what it means: the bond runs both ways; at Anandpur the Guru became disciple to his disciples.
what a scholar hears: the line vaah vaah Gobind Singh aape gur chela is attributed to Bhai Gurdas II (Vaar 41), and 1699 is remembered as the founding of the Khalsa.
